podcast.title: Debut Album
podcast.body: Released in 1965, this debut album was starkly different from mainstream rock and roll which focused on cars and girls; instead, it explored the gritty realities of New York City, including crime, weird sex, strange people, and drugs, which was considered too extreme at the time. Despite selling only about 30,000 copies between 1965 and 1970 and peaking at number 199 on the Billboard Top 200 album charts, its influence was immense, with producer Brian Eno famously stating that everyone who bought a copy started a band. "When their debut album arrived in 1965, rock and roll was largely about cars and girls and various escapists and fun topics. Not the velvet underground. They were from the gritty streets of New York City where there was crime, weird sex, strange people and drugs, lots and lots of drugs."

podcast.body: An acetate pressing from the Scepter Studios Sessions, which predated and contained material for the band's debut album, was discovered and later sold as the most valuable alt-rock collectible. This brittle aluminum acetate could only be played a limited number of times before being destroyed. "These were known as the Scepter Studios Sessions."

srcs.episode: Peaked Too Soon - Bands That Were Ahead of Their Time

podcast.body: Released in March 1967, this album featured Nico and was produced by Andy Warhol, famously sporting a banana on its cover. It is widely considered by many as the beginning of underground, alternative, and experimental music. Recording began in April 1966 at Scepter Studios in New York. The production was quick as most material was already composed from John Cale and Lou Reed's demos. Integrating Nico proved challenging, ultimately leading her to sing some songs due to Warhol's insistence. The album was finished by mid-1966 but delayed due to significant censorship over its strong lyrics about masochism, sexual themes, and drugs (including the song "Heroin"). An executive from Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer initially called it "shit," but ironically, his Verve Records division ultimately released it. Further delays were caused by Warhol's insistence on a peelable banana sticker for the cover, making production expensive and complex. Despite the delays, it was a massive commercial failure upon release, with no promotional support from the record label. "se considera por muchos el inicio de la música underground, posiblemente el inicio de la música alternativa, música experimental."

podcast.body: Released in March 1967, this debut album featured repetitive, drony passages created by John Cale, which had an almost hypnotic effect. Some of the music from this album could be consumed in the dark to create an immersive, carrying-away experience.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: The cover artwork for this album, designed by Andy Warhol, features a banana with the instructions "peel slowly and see." When peeled, the banana skin reveals a flesh-colored banana underneath, inviting interpretation. This type of packaging was very expensive to produce; subsequent editions were unpeelable. Original releases in good condition are highly valuable on the collector's market. A 2008 edition included a sticker to replicate the original effect. "The cover featured a banana with the instructions peel slowly and see. If you peel back the banana skin, you've got a flesh-colored banana. So read into that what you want."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This debut album, credited as being produced by Andy Warhol (though he primarily provided inspiration rather than technical input), was scandalous, shocking, noisy, and angry. Its themes openly addressed sex, drugs, life on the street, S&M, and getting wasted, which was revolutionary for 1967. Despite its explicit content and raw sound, it only reached number 199 on the Billboard Top 200 Chart before disappearing, but it served as a crucial alternative to sugary pop and psychedelic rock for a discerning audience. "The album was just too raw and too real to gain any kind of mainstream attention."

podcast.title: Debut Album
podcast.body: The band's debut album was released in 1967 on Verve, an independent jazz label founded in 1956. Verve decided to take a chance on them largely due to their connection to Andy Warhol. The music was considered "too weird for the mainstream" at a time when rock and roll was primarily about cars and girls, necessitating a move to an indie label with a history of musical experimentation. "The Velvet Underground from their 1967 debut album, which was released on Verve, an independent jazz label founded in 1956, that decided to take a chance on the Velvet's, thanks largely to the group's connection to Andy Warhol."
